items.stimulus: A temporary staffing agency pays a data-entry worker $24 per hour. Last week, the worker earned a total of $840 from this job.
items.stem: At this rate, how many hours did the worker work last week?
items.explanation: You know the total ($840) and the rate ($24 per hour), and you need the time. Time = total ÷ rate, so 840 dollars ÷ 24 dollars/hour = 35 hours. The dollars cancel and hours are left, which tells you the setup is right.

B.why: You subtracted the hourly rate from the total earnings (840 − 24). Subtracting a rate from a total gives no meaningful quantity, and the units do not cancel to hours.

C.why: You added the hourly rate to the total earnings (840 + 24). Dollars per hour cannot be added to dollars. You need to divide.

D.why: You multiplied the total by the rate (840 × 24) when the units say to divide. Your result would be in dollars squared per hour, not hours.

items.stimulus: A hydrologist checks a rain gauge that already holds 1.5 inches of water. A storm then adds rain at a constant rate of 0.4 inch per hour for 6 hours. No water leaves the gauge during the storm.
items.stem: How many inches of water were in the gauge at the end of the storm?

A.why: 13 is the number of 100-kilometer stretches the bird can fly. You still need to convert that to kilometers and then to hours.

C.why: You used all 6.2 grams and didn't hold back the 1.0-gram reserve: $1{,}550 \div 40 = 38.75$.

D.why: 1,300 is the distance in kilometers. The question asks for hours, so divide by 40 km/h.

items.stimulus: A printmaker is pulling an edition of 140 relief prints. Each print uses 2.5 grams of ink. At the start of each printing session, 20 grams of ink is used to charge the roller, and no session can produce more than 40 prints. Ink is sold only in 60-gram tins.
items.stem: What is the minimum number of tins of ink the printmaker must buy to print the entire edition?
items.explanation: The edition needs $140 \div 40 = 3.5$ sessions, so the printmaker must hold 4. The ink needed is $140 \times 2.5 + 4 \times 20 = 350 + 80 = 430$ grams. Then $430 \div 60 \approx 7.17$, so the printmaker must buy 8 tins.

A.why: You counted only the ink on the prints: $350 \div 60 \approx 5.83$, rounded to 6. You left out the 20 grams used to charge the roller in each session.

B.why: You either rounded 7.17 tins down, or you used 3.5 sessions instead of 4, which gives exactly $420 \div 60 = 7$. Sessions are whole events, and a partial tin means buying another one.

D.why: You may have counted 5 sessions, adding a roller charge at the end: $350 + 100 = 450$ grams, which needs 8 tins. Or you may have rounded up twice. Four sessions and 430 grams need 8 tins, not 9.

items.stimulus: A musicologist orders scans of a baroque manuscript from a European archive that charges €3.50 per page. The musicologist has \$500. The bank first deducts a \$20 transfer fee and then converts the rest at 1 U.S. dollar = 0.80 euro.
items.stem: What is the greatest number of complete pages the musicologist can order?
items.explanation: After the fee, $500 - 20 = 480$ dollars is converted. That gives $480 \times 0.80 = 384$ euros. Then $384 \div 3.50 \approx 109.7$, so the musicologist can order 109 complete pages.

B.why: You rounded 109.7 up. The money runs out partway through page 110, so the greatest number of complete pages is 109.

C.why: You converted the whole \$500 before the fee came out: $400 \div 3.50 \approx 114.3$. The \$20 fee is deducted first.

D.why: You divided by 0.80 when you should have multiplied, which turned \$480 into 600 euros. Check the units: dollars × (euros per dollar) gives euros, and a euro is worth more than a dollar, so you should get fewer euros than dollars.

items.subtype_name: Constant rate: rate × time (or amount ÷ rate)
items.stimulus: A steel test plate is 6.0 millimeters thick when installed. In a corrosive environment it loses thickness at a constant rate of 40 micrometers every 6 months ($1 \text{ millimeter} = 1{,}000 \text{ micrometers}$). The plate must be removed from service once its thickness falls below 70% of its original thickness.
items.stem: What is the greatest whole number of years the plate can remain in service?
items.explanation: The minimum allowed thickness is $0.70 \times 6.0 = 4.2$ mm, so the plate can lose $1.8$ mm, or 1,800 micrometers. The rate is 40 micrometers every half year, which is 80 micrometers per year. Then $1{,}800 \div 80 = 22.5$ years. After 23 years the plate is below the limit, so 22 is the greatest whole number of years.

B.why: You rounded 22.5 up. By the end of year 23 the plate has fallen below 4.2 mm, so it can't still be in service.

C.why: You read the rate as 40 micrometers per year: $1{,}800 \div 40 = 45$. The rate is 40 micrometers every 6 months, which is 80 micrometers per year.

D.why: You divided the 4.2 mm the plate must keep by the yearly loss: $4{,}200 \div 80 = 52.5$. The limit depends on the 1.8 mm the plate is allowed to lose.
